idiom_name: traits with associated items, bounds and blanket impls (monomorphised static dispatch)
implementation_notes: Rust's traits are this pattern built into the language: a trait declares the associated types, constants and functions that describe a capability, impl Trait for Type binds them, and generic code selects behaviour with where T: Trait - resolved at compile time by monomorphisation, with no vtable and no common base type. Associated types carry exactly the payload a C++ traits class carries (Iterator::Item), supertraits and where Self: Sized express requirements between traits, and blanket impls (impl<T: Display> ToString for T) play the role of a primary template's default mapping. The classic form is not needed, but retroactive description of a foreign type is impossible: the orphan rule forbids implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type, so a third-party type must be wrapped in a newtype or described by a trait of your own, and stable Rust has no specialization, so a blanket impl plus a more specific impl of the same trait is rejected (RFC 1210 is still the design, not a feature).
pitfalls: Coherence blocks the non-intrusive promise: impl YourTrait for Vec<u8> is rejected when both are foreign, so a type you do not own must be wrapped in a newtype (losing its inherent methods) or described by a local trait you define.

No specialization on stable: a blanket impl and a more specific impl of the same trait cannot coexist, so 'default behaviour refined for some types' must be re-expressed with an internal helper trait, an enum, or a runtime check.

Trait objects (dyn Trait) require a dyn-compatible trait - no generic methods, no associated types with generics, no methods needing Self: Sized - and give up static dispatch, so choosing where T: Trait over Box<dyn Trait> is a real tradeoff rather than a detail.
